title: Power — how fast energy gets transferred
examTip: Power is measured in watts (W). 1 W = 1 J/s. Don't mix up power (the rate of energy transfer) with energy (the total amount transferred).
introTips: Power is about how fast energy is transferred. It is not about how much energy in total.
A weightlifter who raises a barbell slowly does the same work as one who raises it quickly. But the faster one has more power.
Watts and joules per second are the same thing: 1 W = 1 J/s.
intro: A crane that lifts a car in 5 seconds is more powerful than one that takes 20 seconds. Yet both do exactly the same job. Power tells you how quickly energy is transferred. It is why a sports car feels different to a city car. That is true even if both reach the same speed in the end. It is also why a 2 kW kettle boils water faster than a 1 kW one. And it is why power stations are rated in megawatts. Power lets you compare machines, work out costs and solve real exam questions.

basics.text: Energy is what is needed to make things happen. It makes things move, heat up, light up or make a sound. You cannot see energy, but you can see what it does.
Energy is measured in joules, written J. One joule is a small amount, so big amounts are given in kilojoules (kJ). 1 kJ is 1000 J.
A rate tells you how much happens each second. Speed is a rate: how many metres you travel each second.
A force is a push or a pull. Kicking a ball and lifting a bag are both forces. Forces are measured in newtons (N).
Kilo means a thousand: 1 kilometre is 1000 metres. Mega means a million. Giga means a thousand million.
Physics equations use time in seconds. There are 60 seconds in a minute and 3600 seconds in an hour.

keyPoints.heading: What power means
keyPoints.content: Power is the rate at which energy is transferred. It is also the rate at which work is done. It is how much energy transfer happens per second. The equation is: P = E/t (power = energy transferred ÷ time). The unit of power is the watt (W). 1 W = 1 joule per second. You can also write it as P = W/t, where W is work done (in joules). A powerful machine doesn't always transfer more energy overall. It transfers the same energy in a shorter time. Example: a crane lifting a car does the same work whether it takes 5 seconds or 20 seconds. It transfers the same energy. But the crane that does it in 5 seconds has four times the power. The time is divided by 4, so the power is multiplied by 4.
writeBullets: Power — the rate at which energy is transferred, or the rate at which work is done
Watt (W) — the unit of power. 1 W = 1 J/s
P = W/t — power also equals work done (J) ÷ time (s)
More powerful = the same energy transferred in less time, OR more energy in the same time

keyTerms.def: The rate of energy transfer; P = E/t; unit: watts (W)
The unit of power; 1 W = 1 joule per second (1 J/s)
How quickly something happens — here, how many joules transferred per second

keyPoints.memTip: P = E/t. Power is 'energy per second'.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Power and energy are easy to mix up. For the same water, a 2 kW kettle transfers energy twice as fast as a 1 kW kettle. Ignoring energy dissipated to the surroundings, it boils the water in half the time.

keyPoints.heading: Calculating power
keyPoints.content: The main equation is P = E/t. Rearrangements: E = Pt (energy = power × time) and t = E/P (time = energy ÷ power). Worked example 1: a light bulb transfers 100 J in 10 s → P = 100 ÷ 10 = 10 W. Over 3 minutes (= 180 s) it transfers 1800 J. P = 1800 ÷ 180 = 10 W again. Worked example 2: a runner does 12,000 J of work in 60 s → P = 12,000 ÷ 60 = 200 W. Worked example 3: how long does a 2 kW (2000 W) heater take to transfer 36,000 J? t = E/P = 36,000 ÷ 2000 = 18 s. Unit conversions you must know: 1 kW = 1000 W. 1 MW = 1,000,000 W. Always convert to standard units (W and s) before calculating.
writeBullets: P = E/t — power (W) = energy transferred (J) ÷ time (s)
1 kW = 1000 W. Always convert kilowatts to watts before calculating
1 MW = 1,000,000 W. Used for large power stations and factory equipment

keyTerms.def: Power equals energy divided by time; rearranges to E = Pt and t = E/P
1000 watts — unit used for powerful appliances and small generators
1,000,000 watts — unit used for power stations and large industrial outputs

keyPoints.memTip: Triangle trick: put E at the top, and P and t at the bottom. Cover what you want to find: P = E/t, E = Pt, t = E/P.
keyPoints.tutor_note: It is easy to forget to convert minutes to seconds, or kW to W. Make a unit check a habit.

keyPoints.heading: Power in everyday contexts
keyPoints.content: Putting real numbers on power helps you make sense of the world. A higher power means more joules are transferred each second. - Hairdryer: ~2000 W (2 kW). - Electric kettle: ~2000–3000 W. - Electric car motor: 100–300 kW. - Large power station: ~1–2 GW (gigawatts = 1,000,000,000 W).
writeBullets: Hairdryer or kettle — ~2 kW. High power to heat air or water quickly
Electric car motor — 100–300 kW. Very powerful and very efficient
Power station — hundreds of MW to GW. Gigawatts are needed to power whole cities

keyTerms.def: 1,000,000,000 watts — unit used for national power output and very large power stations

keyPoints.memTip: A hairdryer = 2000 W, an electric car = 100,000 W. Scale matters!

keyPoints.heading: Work done
keyPoints.content: Work done (W) = force (F) × distance moved along the line of action of the force (s). Units: joules (J). When a force moves an object, energy is transferred. We say 'work is done'. One joule of work is done when a force of one newton causes a displacement of one metre. So 1 J = 1 N m (one newton-metre). To convert, 20 N m is the same as 20 J. When work is done, energy moves between stores: - lifting an object: work done fills its gravitational potential store - pushing an object against friction: work done against friction goes to the thermal store. This raises the temperature of the object Worked example: a force of 3000 N moves a car 20 m along the line of action of the force. W = Fs = 3000 × 20 = 60,000 J = 60 kJ.
writeBullets: Work done W = Fs. Force (N) × distance moved along the line of action of the force (m) = joules (J)
Energy is transferred when a force moves an object
1 J of work is done when a force of 1 N causes a displacement of 1 m. So 1 J = 1 N m
Work done against friction raises the temperature of the object
Example: 3000 N force over 20 m → W = 60,000 J = 60 kJ

keyTerms.def: W = Fs; energy transferred when a force moves an object, where s is the distance moved along the line of action of the force; unit: joule (J)
1 N m = 1 J; the work done when a force of 1 N causes a displacement of 1 m

keyPoints.memTip: W = Fs. Force times distance gives work done. 1 N m = 1 J.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Say which store the energy goes to. Lifting fills the gravitational potential store. Friction fills the thermal store.

0.question: Crane A lifts a car in 20 s. Crane B lifts the same car to the same height in 5 s. Which statement is correct?
options: Crane B has four times the power of crane A
Crane B transfers four times as much energy as crane A
Both cranes have the same power
Crane A has four times the power of crane B
0.correctFeedback: Correct! Both cranes transfer the same energy. Crane B does it in a quarter of the time, so its power is four times bigger.
0.wrongFeedback: Both cranes do the same work. Power = energy ÷ time. Crane B takes a quarter of the time, so it has four times the power.

1.question: A runner does 18,000 J of work in 90 seconds. What is their power output?
1.correctFeedback: Correct! P = E/t = 18,000 ÷ 90 = 200 W. That is a sensible value for a runner.
1.wrongFeedback: Use P = E/t. Substitute: P = 18,000 J ÷ 90 s = 200 W. Remember to divide energy by time in seconds.

2.question: A hairdryer has a power of 2000 W. A kettle has a power of 2500 W. Which transfers more energy each second?
options: The kettle, because its power is higher
The hairdryer, because it heats air
They transfer the same energy each second
You cannot tell without knowing the time
2.correctFeedback: Correct! Power is the energy transferred each second. The kettle has the higher power, so it transfers more energy each second.
2.wrongFeedback: Power tells you how much energy is transferred each second. 2500 W means 2500 J every second. That is more than 2000 W.

3.question: A force of 50 N pushes a box 4 m along the line of action of the force. How much work is done?
3.wrongFeedback: Use W = Fs (work done = force × distance). W = 50 N × 4 m = 200 J. Multiply, don't divide or add.

commonMistakes: Mixing up power (rate of energy transfer, W) with energy (total amount transferred, J). They are different quantities with different units.
Forgetting to convert minutes to seconds, or kW to W, before calculating. Always work in SI units (W and s).
Thinking a more powerful device always transfers more energy. It transfers energy faster, not always more in total.
Leaving the unit off the answer. Power must be in W (or kW or MW, with conversion), not J or N.
examTips: P = E/t. If you see 'how fast' or 'rate of energy transfer', think power. If you see 'how much total energy', think E = Pt.
Convert units before calculating: kW → W (×1000), minutes → seconds (×60). Write the conversion step out clearly.
If a question gives you efficiency and power together, find the useful output power. It equals efficiency × input power.
